questions.question: Describe how indigenous peoples of South Africa used plants to cure diseases, giving three examples.
questions.expected_answer: Over centuries, the San, Khoikhoi and African farming communities learned which of South Africa's many plants could heal, using leaves, roots, bark, bulbs, flowers and seeds as teas, mixtures, powders, ointments or smoke. The bitter aloe's juice treats stomach problems and its gel is used on burns and skin. Buchu was used for stomach and bladder problems and wounds. Wild wormwood is made into tea for coughs, colds, flu and fevers.

questions.question: Explain how umckaloabo and hoodia show the link between indigenous knowledge and modern medicine.
questions.expected_answer: Healers in the Eastern Cape and Lesotho used umckaloabo roots for coughs and chest problems; in the early nineteen hundreds an Englishman took it to Europe, and today companies there make cough and bronchitis medicines from it. San hunters chewed hoodia to reduce hunger and thirst, and when companies wanted to use it in weight-loss products, the San insisted on benefiting, leading to a 2003 agreement to share any money made.

questions.question: Why must medicinal plants and indigenous knowledge be protected?
questions.expected_answer: Many plants are collected from the wild and sold in markets, and over-harvesting or stripping bark can make them rare, like the pepper-bark tree, so growing them in gardens and nurseries helps. Indigenous knowledge belongs to the communities that discovered it, so the law says companies must get their agreement and share benefits. Plants must also be used safely, because some are poisonous and the right amount matters.
